title: {{NAME}} and the Fossil Code
moral: Different ways of understanding the world can solve what none alone could crack.

pages.content: The Dig Site Seven had been silent for decades before {{NAME}} arrived, and you could feel the silence in the ground itself, a thick, layered quiet like sediment over something important. The site occupied a broad valley carved by an ancient river, its exposed cliff faces striped in ochre and rust and dusty white, each stripe a different age of the world stacked like the pages of a very old book. {{NAME}} was here because DREDGE-4, the excavation robot, had sent an unusual signal. DREDGE-4 was a squat, powerful machine built like a mechanical armadillo, with rotating drill-arms and sensors so precise it could detect the shadow of a bone fragment through three metres of compressed rock. It had found something it described in its report as 'an anomalous pattern inconsistent with geological data.' In the middle of the valley floor, crouched beside an exposed rock face, DREDGE-4 waited with the patient stillness of a machine that has been waiting exactly as long as it calculated it would need to wait. Around it, drifting with evident curiosity through the site, were seven or eight tiny fairy-lights.

pages.content: DREDGE-4 had drilled a careful square around the anomaly, and what lay within it was baffling. It was not a fossil exactly, or not only a fossil. It was a set of tracks pressed into what had once been soft riverbed mud, then hardened to stone over a hundred million years. The tracks were enormous and three-toed. Unmistakably dinosaur. But woven between them, in the preserved mud, was a second set of marks that DREDGE-4 could not classify: tiny indentations in complex repeating patterns, like a code written in a language the robot's database did not contain. 'I have run forty-seven analyses,' DREDGE-4 said, its drill-arms folded in a posture {{NAME}} had come to associate with robot frustration. 'No match found.' One of the fairies, a tiny blue-white spark named Fen, landed in the rock face and placed both hands flat against it. She went very still, the way someone goes still when they are listening to something far away. 'She can read stone,' said another fairy, hovering near {{NAME}}'s ear, her voice like a tiny bell. 'She always could. It's old writing. Very old.' {{NAME}} looked at the pattern in the stone and felt the hair stand up on his arms.

pages.content: Fen worked for a long time, her hands pressed to the stone, her blue-white light pulsing slowly. DREDGE-4 scanned her as she worked, its sensors recording every pulse, building a database entry labelled, with some ambivalence, 'lithic empathy, unclassified.' {{NAME}} sat on the valley floor and watched, taking notes in his orange-piped vest pocket, sketching the pattern as precisely as he could manage. It was the sketching that helped him first. His pencil found the rhythm of the tiny marks, and his hand began to predict the next symbol before he reached it, the way a melody you have heard before comes back to your fingers before your mind has caught up. 'It repeats,' he said, not quite to anyone. DREDGE-4's sensor-lights snapped to him immediately. 'Define the interval,' the robot said. 'Six marks, then it shifts to eight, then back to six,' said {{NAME}}. DREDGE-4 reran its analyses with this constraint in twelve seconds. 'Navigation,' it said. 'This is a migration record. Embedded in a dinosaur trackway. Something was mapping the routes the herds took, for safekeeping.' Fen lifted her hands from the stone and looked at them with an expression of absolute, ancient awe.

pages.content: What the stone said, as best Fen could translate and {{NAME}} could record, was a route. A hundred-million-year-old road that a vast herd of Parasaurolophus had walked season after season, remembered and preserved in tiny fairy script set into the mud beside their tracks, a collaboration between enormous creatures and infinitesimal ones that had outlasted everything. DREDGE-4 fell silent for longer than {{NAME}} had ever known it to fall silent. When it spoke, its voice was different, the rattle-pebble baritone quieter. 'One hundred million years,' it said. 'This record has been in the earth for one hundred million years and we could not read it without the three of us.' Fen flew a slow circle around the track, trailing a thin thread of blue-white light that settled over the ancient marks like a reverent gesture. The valley caught the evening light and the cliff faces blazed, each stripe glowing with its own deep colour, ochre and rust and white, like a library whose shelves reached from the ground to the sky. {{NAME}} looked at the sketch in his hand and understood, for the first time with his whole body, how deep and crowded and extraordinary the world was beneath his feet.

pages.content: They made camp in the valley as the stars appeared, DREDGE-4 producing, from a compartment {{NAME}} had not previously known it possessed, three folding camp chairs and a small gas stove. It brewed tea with the same precision it applied to drilling, one minute forty seconds at ninety-three degrees. The fairies settled in clusters on DREDGE-4's shoulder plates, their lights dimming slowly toward sleep, tiny lanterns going out one by one. Fen remained awake the longest, sitting on {{NAME}}'s knee, re-reading the sketch he had made with small, satisfied nods. {{NAME}} leaned back in his camp chair and looked up at the same sky the Parasaurolophus herds had walked under, impossibly long ago. DREDGE-4 sat with its drill-arms folded, sensor-lights low, recording the stars in its navigation database. 'What are you adding?' {{NAME}} asked drowsily. 'Context,' said DREDGE-4. It was the most interesting thing the robot had ever said. {{NAME}} closed his eyes and slept under the cliff faces, and he wondered whether anywhere else in those deep striped layers of stone there might be another message, waiting.
